articles.title: In 2023, a Washington, DC man believed he had won a $340 million Powerball jackpot; then the lottery said its website had posted the wrong winning numbers
articles.summary: John Cheeks from Washington, DC thought he had won a $340 million Powerball jackpot until a website error led to a legal battle. Discover the shocking details behind the lawsuit that challenges the lottery's responsibility for posting incorrect winning numbers.
articles.body: Winning a lottery jackpot is usually the kind of moment people imagine for years. For Washington, DC resident John Cheeks, that moment appeared to arrive in January 2023, when the numbers displayed on the DC Lottery website matched those printed on his Powerball ticket. The jackpot was estimated at $340 million. One problem remained: the numbers on the website did not match the numbers drawn in the actual Powerball drawing.What happened next turned a potential jackpot into a legal battle over whether the lottery company could be held liable for posting the wrong numbers on its website. By February 2024, Cheeks had filed lawsuits against the companies, demanding either the prize money or compensation due to the mistake.The numbers that appeared to make him a millionaireAccording to The Guardian, Cheeks bought his Powerball ticket on 6 January 2023, selecting numbers that had personal significance to him, including family birthdays. The following day, the actual Powerball drawing took place. Cheeks did not watch the drawing. Instead, when he checked the DC Lottery website in the early hours of 6 January, he saw what appeared to be the winning combination: 7, 15, 23, 32 and 40, with Powerball number 2. Those were the numbers on his ticket. The jackpot was listed at about $340 million.A website test turns into a legal battleWhen Cheeks attempted to claim the prize, however, lottery officials told him that his ticket was not a winner. According to Justia U.S. Law, he was eventually informed that the numbers he had seen online had been posted accidentally during website testing. Taoti Enterprises, the contractor working on the DC Lottery website, had been carrying out quality-assurance tests involving a change to time-zone settings. In a declaration filed with the court, Taoti project manager Brittany Bailey explained that the test numbers were mistakenly published on the live Powerball website instead of a development version.Timing was important. The numbers had been uploaded on 6 January, the day before the Powerball drawing on 7 January. Therefore, it was impossible for them to be the official numbers drawn during the event. The false numbers remained on the DC Lottery website until 9 January. Cheeks sought clarification over how the mistake occurred and raised questions about the lottery companies’ responsibilities after his numbers were displayed as a winner on the official website.The lawsuit filed by Cheeks was directed at the DC Office of Lottery and Gaming, Powerball, Taoti Enterprises and others. Cheeks’ attorneys claimed that, based on the published numbers, he was entitled to the prize. In addition, they argued that in case the jackpot was not won, Cheeks was eligible to claim damages due to negligence in publishing and maintaining the wrong numbers.Why the case raised bigger questions about lottery systemsThe lawsuit may highlight the gap between online results and the process used to validate a winning ticket. According to the DC Office of Lottery and Gaming, winning tickets had to be validated through its gaming system. The defendants further stated that the numbers on the website were clearly a technical error and not from the draw itself.The Iowa Lottery Board also pointed to another incident that offered some context to the dispute. In November 2023, incorrect Powerball numbers were briefly posted online in Iowa because of a reporting error. The numbers remained on the website for about seven hours, and six tickets were paid prizes based on the incorrect results, adding up to $69. The Iowa Lottery also dealt with other tickets presented during that period, with prizes ranging from $4 to $200. The Iowa incident was still very different from Cheeks’s case, which involved numbers that appeared to show he had won a jackpot worth hundreds of millions of dollars.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fast-food drive-thrus took over American mornings for these key reasons
articles.summary: Fast-food breakfast and the drive-thru have become daily rituals for millions of Americans. A food historian reveals how this once-novel concept became an everyday staple.
articles.body: For millions of Americans, grabbing breakfast or coffee from a fast-food drive-thru is an ordinary part of the morning routine — but not long ago, ordering a meal without leaving the car was a novelty. So how did the drive-thru go from a novel idea to an everyday staple? Convenience and an "on-the-go" lifestyle are two big factors, according to Capri Cafaro, the creator, executive producer and host of "America the Bountiful." MORE AMERICANS NOW EAT IN THEIR CARS THAN EVER BEFORE AS EXPERT REVEALS WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT MODERN LIFE Cafaro spoke with Fox News Digital about how and why the drive-thru, particularly drive-thru breakfast, became a daily ritual for many Americans. There is some debate over which restaurant pioneered the drive-thru concept. West Coast chain In-N-Out Burger is widely credited with creating the first drive-thru, debuting a two-way intercom drive-thru system in California in 1948. AMERICA'S LATE-NIGHT FAST-FOOD CULTURE MAY BE MAKING A COMEBACK — HERE'S WHY However, Cafaro and other news publications, maintain that Springfield, Mo., restaurant Red's Giant Hamburg (the word "hamburger" reportedly didn't fit on the sign) actually introduced the drive-thru concept in 1947, narrowly beating In-N-Out. Regardless of which establishment first created it, the drive-thru emerged at a time when Americans' relationship with the automobile was rapidly changing. During the mid-20th century, the country saw a surge in automobile usage due to the growth of suburbs and the rise of highways, particularly the interstate system and Route 66, which will celebrate its 100th anniversary in November. More people took to the roads, not just for their daily commute to and from work, but also for road trips and family outings. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS As Americans ended up behind the wheel, "that really created an opportunity for the rise of fast-food restaurants and certainly the drive-thru," Cafaro noted. Despite McDonald's firm grip on the fast-food breakfast market in recent years, it was not the first chain to introduce the morning meal. McDonald's was actually beaten to the punch by Jack in the Box, which debuted breakfast in 1969 with the Breakfast Jack, a sandwich with egg, cheese and ham. articles.title: Americans ordered what were advertised as 'no cost' Covid tests online; prosecutors say their insurance information was then used to bill more than $500 million for services that were never provided
articles.summary: Americans who ordered Covid-19 tests advertised as 'no cost' online during the pandemic were allegedly at the centre of a healthcare fraud scheme that
articles.body: Americans who ordered Covid-19 tests advertised as 'no cost' online during the pandemic were allegedly at the centre of a healthcare fraud scheme that generated more than $500 million in false claims, according to the US Department of Justice. Prosecutors said the company behind the tests used customers’ insurance information to bill government-backed healthcare programmes for medical services that were never provided.Hasan “Lucas” Seyhun, 45, of Miami, Florida, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud. Seyhun was the Chief Operating Officer of New York-based Fast Lab Technologies, LLC, which offered people 'no cost' Covid-19 tests that could be ordered through its website during the pandemic.According to court documents, Fast Lab allegedly used the insurance details provided by customers to submit claims for Covid-19 testing services that had not actually taken place. The claims included services linked to antigen tests, saliva samples and PCR testing. Prosecutors said the company claimed that medical professionals had observed antigen tests, collected saliva samples and conducted PCR testing, even when those services had not been provided.The case centres on how the insurance information of people seeking Covid-19 tests was allegedly used after they placed their orders. Prosecutors said Seyhun worked with previously charged defendants Cemhan “Jimmy” Biricik, Fast Lab’s CEO, and Dr Martin Perlin, the company’s Medical Director, to carry out the scheme. Seyhun also admitted that, as COO, he helped orchestrate the submission of millions of dollars in fraudulent healthcare claims.Over $500 million in false claimsThe US Attorney’s Office for the Eastern District of Michigan said the scheme resulted in more than $500 million in fake claims being submitted to government-backed healthcare programmes. Seyhun admitted that the fraud resulted in at least $35 million in illicit payments.He has agreed to a forfeiture money judgment of $4,313,153. The amount represents the money he personally received from the scheme.Prosecutors also said the company sometimes submitted claims before customers had even received their Covid-19 test kits. US Attorney Jerome F Gorgon Jr said the alleged conduct took advantage of the fear and isolation surrounding the pandemic.“Ripping off the American taxpayer is bad enough. Using the fear and isolation of the Covid pandemic to do it is sickening,” Gorgon said. “Not only did Seyhun and his co-conspirators defraud the American public of hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of fake services, but they were so confident in their scheme that they routinely submitted claims for payment before test kits were even delivered to the customer,” Attorney Gorgon added.According to The Justice Department, Seyhun’s guilty plea was part of a wider investigation into pandemic-related healthcare fraud. The investigation involved several federal and state agencies, including the FBI Detroit Field Office, the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General, the Office of Personnel Management Office of Inspector General and the Michigan Attorney General’s Medicaid Fraud Control Unit.How the billing workedThe alleged fraud involved several types of Covid-19 testing services. Prosecutors said Fast Lab submitted claims stating that antigen tests had been observed by medical professionals. Antigen tests are used to detect proteins from the virus.The company also allegedly claimed that saliva samples had been collected by medical personnel. Those samples were then allegedly billed as having undergone PCR testing. PCR tests detect genetic material from the virus and were widely used for Covid-19 diagnosis during the pandemic.The government said the use of customers’ insurance information allowed the company to seek payments for services connected to tests that people had ordered online.Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the National Fraud Enforcement Division said Seyhun and his colleagues had exploited public trust during the pandemic.“At a time when Americans were scared for their families and their futures, Hasan Seyhun saw an opportunity to turn a national crisis into his own personal payday,” McDonald said. “Instead of providing the American people with the assistance they needed during a critical time, Seyhun and his colleagues exploited their trust, and lined their pockets from fraudulent insurance claims,” he added.The FBI also said the scale of the alleged scheme affected healthcare funding and public trust. Jennifer Runyan, Special Agent in Charge of the FBI Detroit Field Office, said, "A scheme of this magnitude undermines public trust and diverts critical healthcare dollars away from the people and programs who need it most. Today’s guilty plea is an important step toward accountability for conduct that resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in fraudulent billings,” Runyan said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Japan's first named ankylosaur, Nipponopelta yezoensis, was more closely related to North American and European nodosaurids millions of years ago
articles.summary: More than three decades after a partial ankylosaur skull was first discovered in a Hokkaido riverbank deposit, researchers have formally named it as a new
articles.body: More than three decades after a partial ankylosaur skull was first discovered in a Hokkaido riverbank deposit, researchers have formally named it as a new genus and species, Nipponopelta yezoensis, the first ankylosaur ever formally named from Japan. The study, ‘A new nodosaurid ankylosaur (Dinosauria: Ornithischia) from the Upper Cretaceous Hikagenosawa Formation in Japan reveals dispersal pattern of Asian nodosaurid ankylosaurs,’ published in Cretaceous Research, was led by Shumpei Oyabu of Hokkaido University alongside colleagues from Japan, Canada and the United States.Using CT scanning and phylogenetic analysis, the researchers resolved the specimen's identity and uncovered an unexpected evolutionary relationship with nodosaurids from North America and Europe. Here's how the fossil was rediscovered, and what it reveals about how armoured dinosaurs were distributed across ancient continents.A Hokkaido fossil in storage, how the specimen was finally identifiedA partial skull, the atlas, or first cervical vertebra, and several teeth, catalogued as MCM A522, were discovered in a concretion from the Hikagenosawa Formation along the Omakizawa River, a tributary of the Shuparo River in Yubari, Hokkaido, and donated to the Mikasa City Museum by Eijiro Goto. The specimen was first described in 2005 by Hayakawa and colleagues, who identified it as a nodosaurid ankylosaur based on its teeth and occipital bone morphology, but its precise taxonomic position remained unresolved for years. Acid preparation and the limited exposure of teeth preserved within the skull made detailed morphological study difficult.What CT scanning revealed about the new speciesTo finally resolve the specimen's identity, Oyabu and colleagues applied three-dimensional CT reconstruction, digitally revealing parts of the skull that had previously remained hidden, including a section of the lower jaw, two intact teeth and the dinosaur's left inner ear. The scans exposed a distinctive combination of features in the back of the skull, unique enough to justify naming a new taxon, Nipponopelta yezoensis. The specimen is particularly important because it is the only Asian nodosaurid currently known from skull elements; other Asian nodosaurids are known only from postcranial material, making it an important reference point for understanding the group's anatomy.A surprising family tree, closer to North America than AsiaRather than grouping with the handful of other nodosaurids previously described from Asia, phylogenetic analysis placed Nipponopelta yezoensis deeply within derived North American and European nodosaurids, including Pawpawsaurus, Panoplosaurus, Nodosaurus, Edmontonia and Denversaurus, as well as the European taxon Dracopelta. This unexpected placement showed that Nipponopelta was more closely related to these North American and European forms than to other Asian nodosaurids, prompting the researchers to examine how different nodosaurid lineages may have become distributed across regions over millions of years.How Nipponopelta's ancestors spread across continentsAncestral geographic analysis suggested that the lineage containing Nipponopelta yezoensis and its close relatives had a broad ancestral distribution spanning Laramidia, Appalachia and Asia. Habitat reconstruction further showed that Nipponopelta yezoensis preferred marine-influenced environments, likely inhabiting coastal or estuarine areas. The researchers suggested that this coastal preference may have played an important role in shaping its dispersal patterns across different regions. The Hikagenosawa Formation itself, part of the mostly marine Yezo Group, has also previously yielded other significant dinosaur finds, including the hadrosaurid Kamuysaurus japonicus and the therizinosaurid Paralitherizinosaurus japonicus. Together, these discoveries add to the importance of Hokkaido's Cretaceous rocks for understanding dinosaur diversity in ancient marine-influenced environments million years ago.You use AI every day. articles.title: Omar’s resolution on J&K’s statehood fuels autonomy debate in J&K House
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah today brought a resolution before Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly seeking the restoration
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Omar Abdullah today brought a resolution before Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly seeking the restoration of full statehood to Jammu and Kashmir. However, the resolution was fiercely opposed by the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) creating chaotic scenes forcing the speaker to adjourn the House.As the resolution contains a reference to the autonomy resolution passed by J&K Assembly in June 2000, when Jammu and Kashmir was a state, the BJP accused the ruling party of being anti-national and called the resolution an autonomy resolution.Omar’s resolution reads: "In addition to the resolutions passed by this House on 26 June 2000 and 6 November 2024, the House calls upon the Government of India for the immediate and urgent restoration of full statehood to Jammu and Kashmir and resolves that this resolution be forwarded to the Government of India."For nearly two years, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah has repeatedly called for the restoration of statehood and taken up the issue with the Centre. Soon after taking office, his Cabinet passed a resolution seeking restoration of statehood.NC legislators said the Centre’s lack of movement on statehood forced the party to bring the resolution in the Assembly. Omar echoed this, saying it seems the cabinet was not seen as the sole voice of the people, while the legislature represented the broader political spectrum of Jammu and Kashmir including parties outside the government. “Statehood is not about the government or my family, it is about Jammu and Kashmir. That is why we brought it to the House, so that a united voice can go to the Centre for restoration of statehood,” Omar said.After Omar moved the resolution, the BJP legislators shouted slogans, tore copies of the resolution. Incidentally Congress legislators supported the resolution even moved towards the well to confront BJP legislators. The BJP argues that the resolution shouldn’t have mentioned autonomy resolution in the statehood resolution. Angered by the BJP legislators’ slogans, some of the NC legislators displayed papers reading “we want autonomy of J&K be restored.” Others called for restoration of Article 370.Earlier addressing the House after moving the resolution, the CM said the House should discuss and pass the resolution as lack of statehood to J&K is causing immense suffering to people of J&K.“We were promised that the restoration of statehood would follow delimitation and elections. Delimitation of constituencies was carried out. Elections were held and a large number of people took part in them (in 2024). People voted without any coercion. But the third step of the promise, the restoration of statehood was not fulfilled,” Omar said, referring to assurances given by the centre in Parliament and before the Supreme Court.The CM said statehood was a promise made by the government of India and reaffirmed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a function where he was present along with the leader of Opposition in J&K Sunil Sharma. He said the Prime Minister has stated that the restoration of statehood is Modi’s promise.Omar said several important institutions and projects remained beyond the effective control of the elected government, citing the Power Development Corporation and AIIMS-related matters as examples.“As chief minister and power minister, I do not receive the files of the J&K State Power Development Corporation. If the elected government is responsible for everything other than security, law and order, and services matters, then why are institutions like the State Power Development Corporation or health institutions like SKIMS outside its control,"J&K CM added.Explaining the adding previous resolution to the current resolution, he said the House continued to stand by all resolutions passed earlier by the Assembly. He said he has mentioned earlier resolutions in the current resolution so that “our friends” an indirect reference to the PDP shouldn’t say that “we have given up on them.” “Those resolutions remain in place. This House owns them. This resolution neither replaces nor ignores them. It is an addition to them,” he said.Omar said the resolution simply called upon the Government of India to fulfil its commitment and restore full statehood to Jammu and Kashmir. “We do not want a half state, a quarter state or a state without powers over law and order. We were promised full statehood and full statehood is what we seek,” he said.“We wanted a resolution to be passed by the Assembly and sent to the Government of India stating that Jammu and Kashmir’s statehood should be restored immediately,” he said.Later talking to reporters Omar said, “elections were held almost two years ago and a promise was made to restore statehood to Jammu and Kashmir.” He said the promise has not been fulfilled. “We are asking the BJP to vote only on statehood. We are not asking them to vote on Article 370, special status or autonomy. Those resolutions have already been passed by this House.”The chief minister rejected BJP’s accusation that his resolution is an anti-national stating, “how can demanding statehood be anti-national? What is anti-national about it? We have not brought a resolution on autonomy. Those resolutions have already been passed by the House. They remain the property of the House. We are not touching them. This new resolution is only about restoring statehood and does not dilute the earlier resolutions.” However, he said, if the BJP wants to bring a resolution to replace or reject the earlier resolutions, they should do it. “We are a democracy.”Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2005, Missy Hammerstrom gave a Louisville child her apple for the weekend; Blessings in a Backpack later provided 30 million hunger-free weekends to more than 1 million children
articles.summary: Discover how a simple act of kindness led to the creation of Blessings in a Backpack, providing 30 million hunger-free weekends for over 1 million children across the US since 2005. Learn about the impact and growth of this vital program.
articles.body: In 2005, a simple request from a child at a Louisville elementary school gave Missy Hammerstrom a glimpse of a problem that could easily go unnoticed. While having lunch with students, Hammerstrom was asked if she could give a young girl her apple. When she asked why, the child explained that she wanted to take it home so she would have something to eat over the weekend. That small moment helped inspire Blessings in a Backpack, which says it has since provided 30 million hunger-free weekends to more than 1 million children across the United States.According to Blessings in a Backpack, Hammerstrom was volunteering at an elementary school in Louisville, Kentucky, in 2005 when a little girl asked for her apple because she wanted to take it home for the weekend, saying she did not have enough to eat. The encounter inspired Hammerstrom to take action. She cleared space in her garage, bought backpacks, filled them with food and donated them to the school. That first effort fed 30 children that weekend. From those first backpacks, Blessings in a Backpack grew into a national organisation providing food to children over weekends.From one Louisville school to a national programmeWorking with community leaders and a Louisville philanthropist, Hammerstrom founded the first Blessings in a Backpack program at Roosevelt Perry Elementary School. The program spread throughout Louisville and Kentucky before being launched in other states. In December 2008, Blessings in a Backpack launched the first program outside Kentucky and incorporated as a 501(c)(3) charitable organisation. Children who might otherwise face food shortages over the weekend receive food to take home on Friday, helping bridge the period when school-based meals are unavailable. The organisation says its mission is to mobilise communities, individuals and resources to provide weekend food for school-aged children who might otherwise go hungry.However, the programme has grown considerably since those early days. According to Blessings in a Backpack, during the 2024–2025 academic year, more than 2.7 million bags of ready-to-eat food were distributed to children at nearly 1,000 schools across the US. The programme has also expanded to more than 1,200 community initiatives nationwide. The organisation also states that its work since 2009 has helped more than 1 million children and provided 30 million hunger-free weekends.Why the weekend gap mattersThese programmes are designed to fill a gap that appears when the school week ends. Children may receive breakfast and lunch at school during the week, but those meals are not provided on Saturdays and Sundays. For families already trying to stretch their budgets, covering those extra meals can add another challenge.There is also growing interest in whether weekend food programmes can offer benefits beyond putting food on the table. Blessings in a Backpack conducted its own evaluation in collaboration with Ipsos and Quaker Oats, with participants reporting that they felt cared for by their community and found it easier to focus on school. These responses point to possible wider benefits, although they do not by themselves establish that the programme was the direct cause.A legacy that outgrew one appleIn 2018, Hammerstrom’s family joined Louisville volunteers to distribute more than 400 food-filled bags at Engelhard Elementary School. The city also honoured her work by declaring September 29, 2018, as Missy Hammerstrom Day. Hammerstrom had died in 2010, but her family continued to take part in the effort, keeping her connection to the programme alive.Her story is also a reminder that community efforts can take on a life of their own. What began as a local response to a child’s need eventually became a much larger organisation, with volunteers, schools and communities across the country taking part. By the time her family returned to Engelhard Elementary in 2018, the programme had moved well beyond its Louisville beginnings, while still carrying the same basic idea of making sure children had food to take home for the weekend.You use AI every day. articles.title: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV's historic France visit includes a private meeting with abuse victims in Lourdes and a Saturday Mass expecting up to 1 million people.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008. French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds. "Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history." POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility." In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability. SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants, the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity. French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile. Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II, on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia. Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right. POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not." The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China. Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks. He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend. Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: No action taken against Iranian man who tried to enter nuclear base
articles.summary: The 34-year-old was  arrested in March after trying to access the Faslane base in Argyll and Bute, home to the Royal Navy's nuclear submarine fleet.
articles.body:
No action is to be taken against an Iranian man who tried to enter the Faslane nuclear submarine base earlier this year.

The 34-year-old was arrested at HM Naval Base Clyde near Helensburgh, Argyll and Bute, on 19 March, along with a 31-year-old Romanian woman.

The Crown Office said it had carefully considered the case and decided there should be no further proceedings against the man.

It had previously said in March that no proceedings would be brought against the Romanian woman.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

The man had been charged, but was later released pending further inquiries without appearing in court.

Faslane, on the Gare Loch about 25 miles (40km) north-west of Glasgow, is the home of the Royal Navy's nuclear-powered submarine fleet.

Those include the UK's four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines which carry Trident nuclear missiles.

The March arrests came a few weeks after the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February.

The Crown Office said: "The Procurator Fiscal received a report relating to a 34-year-old man and an incident said to have occurred on 19 March 2026.

"After careful consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, including the available admissible evidence, the procurator fiscal decided that there should be no proceedings taken at this time.

"The Crown reserves the right to proceed in the future should further evidence become available."

articles.title: Jay-Z rape accuser formally withdraws allegation
articles.summary: A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 now says she has never met the rap superstar.
articles.body:
A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.

The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.

The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.

In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."

The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.

"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."

Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".

When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer Beyoncé, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."

The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.

She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.

The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.

In a statement to Rolling Stone , which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.

He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."

When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".

In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."

Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said.

She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said.

She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".

She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false."

Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs.

Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit".

The BBC has contacted Buzbee for comment.

In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence.

articles.title: A retired UK rail engineer turned his East Sussex garden into a working railway using a Victorian platelayer’s trolley; the line now runs 50 feet and uses a 12-volt battery charged by solar power
articles.summary: A former railway engineer has transformed his garden in East Sussex into an unusual working railway, complete with full-size track, a vintage-style
articles.body: A former railway engineer has transformed his garden in East Sussex into an unusual working railway, complete with full-size track, a vintage-style carriage and railway memorabilia. Railway Magazine, which featured Adrian Backshall’s project, describes the 50-foot line as a Wickham lookalike built on an old platelayer’s trolley. The small railway now uses a 12-volt car battery charged by a solar panel to power its winch, allowing the carriage to travel slowly along the garden track. What began as a lockdown project has since grown into a distinctive railway-themed garden attraction for Backshall, his family and guests.From railway career to garden railwayAdrian Backshall retired from Network Rail in 2018 after a career working on Britain's railways. His connection with railway equipment, however, did not end with retirement. During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex. The project gave him a way to put his railway knowledge and collection of equipment to use while spending more time at home. The centrepiece is a carriage based on a Victorian platelayer's trolley. A friend who was a blacksmith helped create the Wickham-style body that sits on top of the original trolley.Platelayers' trolleys were lightweight railway vehicles historically used by railway workers to travel along tracks while carrying tools and equipment. Backshall's version retains the character of such a vehicle while giving it a new purpose as a garden railway carriage.A 50-foot railway in the gardenWhat started as a much shorter line has now become a 50-foot railway running through the garden. Some of the track used in the project dates back to 1898, giving the otherwise modern garden installation a genuine connection with railway history. Backshall has also added railway signs, signals and other pieces of equipment around the property, making the garden resemble a miniature railway museum.The railway has two main stopping points, near the garden shed and patio. The line is not designed for speed. Instead, the carriage moves slowly enough for passengers to enjoy the unusual surroundings as it makes its journey through the garden. According to Railway Magazine, the 50-foot cable-worked railway has a maximum speed of about 0.3 miles per hour. That extremely slow pace is part of the charm of the project. Rather than trying to recreate a conventional railway journey, Backshall has created something closer to a moving garden room with a genuine railway feel.From hand power to solar energyThe railway has also evolved technically since its early days. Initially, the carriage was moved using a hand-cranked pulley arrangement. As the project expanded, Backshall replaced that system with a 12-volt winch. The winch is powered by a 12-volt car battery, which is charged using a solar panel. This allows the railway to operate without relying on a conventional mains-powered system for its movement.The arrangement combines old railway equipment with simple modern technology. A Victorian-era trolley forms the basis of the carriage, while solar power provides the energy needed to move it along the track. The result is a small but functioning railway that reflects Backshall's interest in both railway history and engineering.Railway memorabilia fills the gardenThe track is only part of the transformation. Backshall's garden contains a collection of authentic railway-related objects, including signs, signals and other equipment. Some of the signs retain the language associated with working railway lines, giving visitors the impression that they have stepped into a small railway installation rather than an ordinary residential garden.Inside the carriage, the railway theme continues. The cabin has seating for four people and includes a wood-burning stove, while railway memorabilia and other details make the space suitable for entertaining. Backshall and his wife Ruth have used the train for gatherings and tea parties, turning the unusual railway into part of their home life. The project has also involved some negotiation over space. As the railway was extended, the track passed through part of the garden that had previously been used for flowers. Ruth has spoken about the changes with humour, while supporting the project that began as a lockdown idea.A lockdown project that kept growingBackshall's railway demonstrates how a small hobby can develop into a much more elaborate personal project. The original lockdown railway was considerably shorter, but the line has since been extended to 50 feet. The addition of a solar-powered winch has also made the operation more convenient than the original hand-powered arrangement. For someone who spent decades around Britain's railways, the project offers a way to preserve that connection after retirement. Instead of simply displaying an old trolley, Backshall has incorporated it into a functioning railway environment. The garden railway has also attracted wider attention. Backshall and Ruth held an open day in June 2025 to raise money for St Wilfrid's Hospice, allowing the unusual project to serve a charitable purpose as well.Today, the 50-foot line stands as an unusual combination of railway history, engineering and gardening. With its Victorian trolley, historic track, railway signs and solar-powered 12-volt system, Backshall's creation has turned an ordinary East Sussex garden into a working piece of railway heritage.You use AI every day. articles.title: Jamie Dimon donates $12 million to 12 historically Black colleges and universities, joining billionaires filling the gap after US government pulled back funding for public institutions, HBCUs; here's what foundation's statement says ...
articles.summary: Jamie Dimon, CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase along with his wife Judith have donated $12 million via the James and Judith K.
articles.body: Jamie Dimon, CEO of America’s largest bank JPMorgan Chase along with his wife Judith have donated $12 million via the James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation to support 12 historically Black colleges and universities (HBCUs). According to a report by Fortune, the gift announced by the United Negro College Fund (UNCF), establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and comes amid shrinking federal support for public institutions and HBCUs. Rather than funding a single program, the Dimon donation flows into permanent endowments, giving schools long-term financial stabilityWhat James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation said about the donationIn a joint statement, Jamie and Judith Dimon said: “Our system of HBCUs continue to serve as the springboard to success for thousands of students in pursuit of the American Dream. As the children of first-generation high school and college graduates, we were imbued with a thirst for knowledge and a drive to succeed—principles that we have passed on to our own children and that we wish to share with all the students at the selected HBCUs.”The gift, and where it's goingThe James and Judith K. Dimon Foundation's donation was announced by the United Negro College Fund (UNCF) on August 20. The gift establishes the Dimon Fund to Advance Economic Opportunity and is part of UNCF's broader $1.5 billion capital campaign, providing permanent endowment capital to the selected schools as part of a $5 million institutional match drawn from UNCF's pooled endowment fund.The 12 recipient institutions are Benedict College, Dillard University, Edward Waters University, Huston-Tillotson University, Jarvis Christian University, Johnson C. Smith University, Miles College, Oakwood University, Shaw University, Stillman College, Tuskegee University, and Voorhees University.UNCF said the schools were chosen specifically for their leadership and strong track records preparing teachers, nurses, and other healthcare professionals — fields where HBCUs have historically excelled at supporting first-generation students.Jamie Dimon donates directly into permanent endowmentsRather than funding a single initiative, the Dimons' donation flows directly into permanent endowments. UNCF argues this structure gives schools the flexibility to plan years or even decades ahead, rather than having to scramble annually for fresh donations to sustain existing programs.In a joint statement, Jamie and Judith Dimon described HBCUs as a longstanding springboard toward the American Dream for thousands of students, tying the gift to their own family history as children of first-generation high school and college graduates who were raised with a strong drive toward education and success — values they said they've since passed on to their own children and hope to extend to students at the selected schools.Jamie Dimon’s quieter philanthropic patternWhile Dimon is widely known for his tenure leading JPMorgan Chase, the world's largest bank, and for his frequent commentary on the economy and workplace culture, his philanthropic work through the Dimon Foundation is considerably less publicized. The foundation, established in 1996, doesn't even maintain its own website, but according to ProPublica data drawn from its most recent tax filing, it distributed more than $9 million in 2024 alone, largely toward organizations focused on public education and career advancement.That focus lines up with the foundation's other work: Judith Dimon, who serves as its president, oversees grantmaking centered on career-connected learning for New York City public school students, and the foundation helped launch FutureReadyNYC, an initiative aiming to give 100,000 students hands-on career experience by 2030. Jamie Dimon has also previously served on UNCF's board.The donation from Jamie Dimon arrives at a moment when federal funding for HBCUs and other public institutions has grown increasingly uncertain under the Trump administration. Other billionaire philanthropists have moved to fill similar gaps — most notably MacKenzie Scott, who has donated more than $700 million to over a dozen HBCUs and affiliated organizations in recent years.You use AI every day. articles.title: Some BBC channels and radio stations 'may well' have to close, director general says
articles.summary: The BBC's financial situation "may well mean" some channels and stations close, Matt Brittin says.
articles.body:
The BBC's financial situation and changing audience habits "may well mean" some channels and radio stations have to close so resources can be invested in on-demand services, its director general has said.

As the BBC seeks £500m savings, Matt Brittin told BBC One's Sunday With Laura Kuenssberg that "we wouldn't guarantee any programme or any channel will exist forever".

He said: "The tight financial situation means that we're having to look at some of those decisions a bit sooner than we might like."

Audience behaviour is also rapidly changing, he said. "If most of an audience is getting things on demand, we have to look at the value and the cost of all of those different services."

Brittin said his focus when making savings was to "minimise the impact on audience".

He explained: "We might have some channels and services where maybe 100,000 people are watching the broadcast service but 500,000 are getting those programmes on iPlayer.

"When's the right time to migrate that service fully to being on-demand? And part of my job is to safeguard value for money for the licence fee payer."

The BBC should go "in different ways to reach audiences and we're locked into yesterday's model of how people consume content, and actually the audience is always already living in tomorrow's world", he said.

In recent months, the BBC has announced a series of closures of jobs and programmes including Blankety Blank, Celebrity Mastermind, Live At The Apollo and Football Focus, and further cuts are expected.

Brittin took over as BBC director general in May after a decade as president of Google in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

Asked by Kuenssberg if he would allow a programme to be made and presented by AI, Brittin replied: "I would do, within guardrails."

He added: "We want to experiment with this technology and understand what it can and can't do, but I'm here because I believe in human creativity.

"I don't think anything we do should be replaced by AI. I think there are lots of places where AI can help us make the licence fee go further, but also help us in our decision-making and creativity. But it's not a substitute for humans."

He also warned of the danger of a handful of tech companies having too much control over information in the future.

"We're also in this moment where AI is in takeoff. So I think there's a danger that six companies will control access to information in future and the creation of information and misinformation," he said.

"Six companies, none of them European, let alone British. In that world, here's the BBC. It's the most trusted organisation by over half a billion people."

Asked if he trusted big tech companies he replied: "There's a lot of platforms out there, so I wouldn't trust any platform innately.

"And I think what you do is you keep under review how those things work and whether your content can show up in the right place and fulfil its mission.

"I think the BBC and our apps and services should be the antidote to the algorithm. Everywhere else you go is driven by some commercial interest."

The interview will be available on BBC Sounds and YouTube on Saturday 26 September, then on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg on BBC One and iPlayer at 09:00 BST on 27 September.

articles.title: Underpass in Weymouth gets ocean-inspired makeover
articles.summary: The murals in Westham feature turtles, sharks, jellyfish, seahorses, crabs and an octopus.
articles.body:
An underpass in Weymouth has been given an underwater makeover with vibrant new murals.

The walkway in Westham by the swannery has been decorated by two artists, alongside young people from youth and children's group Hope House.

The first subway mural has been finished and includes crabs, jellyfish, turtles, seahorses, sharks and a large octopus. Artwork on the second subway is now set to get underway.

The murals were funded with a £5,000 community grant awarded to the youth, children's and community centre by Weymouth Town Council in July.

The young people helped develop the theme, create the designs and paint the murals.

Hope House manager Joe Hobday said: "What has been particularly lovely is seeing how proud they are to have actually played a part in creating something that is now a permanent piece of art in our town.

"They have a real sense of ownership over it, and now that people are seeing it, they are all so excited to be able to say 'we helped make that'.

"We are really looking forward to getting involved in finalising the second subway too."

articles.title: Allies unite behind Saudi Arabia as more Iranian flights curtailed
articles.summary: RIYADH/CAIRO, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, w...
articles.body:
FILE PHOTO: Battle between Iran-aligned Houthi fighters and Saudi backed forces in al Jawf governate

RIYADH/CAIRO, Sept 25 (Reuters) - Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani military chiefs are to discuss help for Saudi Arabia as it faces attacks by Yemen's Houthis, while Iraq further curtailed Iranian flights on Friday in line with US pressure, and an Iranian official threatened retaliation.

The Houthis have launched strikes on the Saudi-backed government in ‌Yemen and repeatedly fired into Saudi Arabia, disrupting oil flows from the world's largest energy exporter, as part of a wider Middle East war that began with US and Israeli ‌strikes on Iran on February 28.

The military escalation continued this week despite a push during the UN General Assembly in New York to revive diplomacy to end the conflict, which quickly spread to Lebanon and the Gulf in March before escalating ​in Yemen in recent weeks.

With talks stalled and during a lull in direct fire by the US and Iran, Washington had shifted tactics to extend the reach of its financial sanctions by targeting companies from third countries that do business with Iranian firms through "secondary sanctions".

Iranian airlines were barred from neighbouring countries including the United Arab Emirates and Oman on Thursday in response to new US sanctions, the first big impact of the shift.

On Friday, the three other Iraqi airports that operate flights to and from Iran joined Baghdad airport in suspending them, sources and state media said.

A flight ban, if sustained, could deepen Iran's isolation and worsen an economic crisis ‌in the country, which is already facing a US blockade of its ⁠seaports.

Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran's supreme leader, accused regional countries of "alignment with America" for blocking flights.

"If Iran does not have the possibility to fly and receive airport services, then no country in the region will have this possibility either," he said in a social media post.

The war, which US President ⁠Donald Trump launched alongside Israel, has killed thousands of people and disrupted global trade and energy supplies, adding to inflationary pressures.

While the fighting between the US and Iran has been stop-start, Iranian allies have mobilised, with Hezbollah confronting Israel in Lebanon and the Houthis advancing in Yemen, prompting a new humanitarian crisis.

Iran and its allies have significantly squeezed oil exports from Saudi Arabia, a US ally. The Houthis have disrupted ship traffic at the mouth of the ​Red ​Sea while Iran has effectively limited tanker traffic at the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for 20% of the ​world's oil exports before the war.

On Thursday, the Houthis said they had fired ‌dozens of missiles and drones at Saudi targets, while authorities in Saudi Arabia said they had intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Houthi fighters.

Later, Saudi Arabia's Grand Mufti, the kingdom's top religious authority, called on soldiers to be ready to lay down their lives to fight the Houthis until the group is ousted from power.

Amid the fighting, the Saudi, Pakistani and Turkish foreign ministers met within the framework of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August. They condemned attacks targeting Mecca and other civilian sites, while affirming Saudi Arabia's right to defend itself.

"The ministers also discussed arrangements for holding an urgent meeting of the chiefs of staff of the three countries to discuss ways to support Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which stipulates that an attack against any one of the parties constitutes an attack against all parties," ‌a Saudi statement said.

Turkey's defence ministry said Chief of General Staff General Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would travel to Saudi Arabia ​on Friday to meet his Saudi and Pakistani counterparts.

Ankara has previously said it could help meet Riyadh's military needs, especially on ​technical issues, but officials have said any support at this stage would be largely bilateral and in ​the spirit of their alliance, since the joint defence agreement has not yet been ratified by Turkey's parliament.

In New York, Iran's Foreign ‌Minister Abbas Araqchi told reporters on Thursday that Tehran had conveyed a proposal ​to the US via intermediaries under which the Strait ​of Hormuz would be reopened if Tehran's conditions were met.

Under Iran's proposal, hostilities would end on all fronts, including Lebanon, within seven days. The US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports, release Iran's frozen funds and waive its oil sanctions, he said.

"The Strait of Hormuz will be reopened on the last day," Araqchi said, adding that talks with the US on other issues, ​including Iran's nuclear issue, would then start.

A senior Iranian official told Reuters ‌on Wednesday that Tehran was reviewing Washington's response to its peace proposals.

Oil prices fell on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce, despite the number of ships ​recorded transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropping to nine on Thursday, half the 10-day average.

(Reporting by Timour Azhari in Riyadh, Hatem Maher in Cairo, Kanishka Singh in Washington, Tuvan ​Gumrukcu in Ankara; Writing by Daniel Trotta and Aidan Lewis; Editing by Lincoln Feast, Stephen Coates, and)

articles.title: Democrat politicians are betraying their own voters on trans sports issue
articles.summary: Jean Chadbourne and other registered Democrats say their party is alienating its own base by refusing to protect women's sports from trans athletes.
articles.body: Jean Chadbourne is a registered Democrat who has donated to Joe Biden, Elizabeth Warren and Pete Buttigieg. And she lives in the Bay Area, where she is surrounded by progressives who recoil at the sound of Donald Trump's name. So it probably wouldn't surprise you that she is seething at a certain political party right now. What might surprise you, though — is that that political party is her own. As OutKick’s Jackson Thompson reported, only two Democrats showed up to Wednesday's Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on protecting women's sports, and both left within an hour. The party's leaders weren't on hand to hear testimony from witnesses arguing the need to separate biological males and females in athletic competition, and they called no witnesses of their own. DEMOCRATS STAY QUIET ON NEXT STEPS AFTER SUPREME COURT TRANSGENDER SPORTS RULING Some might say this was an effort to dismiss a Republican talking point designed to rile up the GOP base. But Chadbourne, who regularly attends rallies in support of girls having their own spaces, will tell you that the Democrats are alienating their own constituents. "They're eroding their base," said Chadbourne, who founded Women are Real — a grassroots women's group she says is about 65 percent Democrat. "You would think four years into this I would be prepared for them to continue to die on this hill. However, I again was just struck with how deranged this whole thing was...they didn't even want to argue their case for why boys should be in girls sports." It's no secret that Republican voters are largely against the inclusion of trans athletes in girls and women's sports. What might be less known is that most Democrat voters are, too. A New York Times poll from last year showed that 67 percent of people who lean Dem oppose the mixing of the two sexes in sports, while a Pew poll said 55 percent of Democrats would be "not too" or "not at all" comfortable with athletes playing on teams that don't match their sex at birth. Yet Democrat politicians seem to disregard this substantial portion of their base. Or they do what Virginia governor Abigail Spanberger did in July, which was to roll back proposed protections for biological females sports without announcing it to the public. It's as though they know their actions (or lack thereof) will cause a stir among their constituents, so they navigate the issue as clandestinely as possible. But why? Kara Dansky, another registered Democrat, has some theories. In 2023, Dansky wrote a book called "The Reckoning: How the Democrats and the Left Betrayed Women and Girls." And one point she's made repeatedly is how there is a "multi-billion industry" motivated to make gender-transitioning as frequent as possible. "A lot of kids are being put on a lot of drugs, which, if they go the traditional route, they will take for decades if not the rest of their lives," said Dansky, a lawyer who also attends rallies supporting the separation of sexes in sports. "So we're putting a large chunk of the young generation on a lifetime's worth of hormones." Her point? There is a well-funded lobbying effort that could be influencing lawmakers. This, of course, is not something that can be confirmed at the moment. What's undeniable, though, is Trump's opposition to trans athletes in female sports. And the President is a bit of a magician in this regard — if he's for something, he can instantly turn the Democrats against it. Former Democrat Jennifer Sey — the founder of XX-XY Athletics — couldn't help but zero in on this. She is convinced that the Democrat politicians are guided not by the public, but by Trump-deranged staffers who influence their every decision. SUPREME COURT MAKES RULING ON TRANS ATHLETES IN WOMEN'S SPORTS Part of the reason she left the party was because its leaders couldn't define what a woman is. How many more will walk away over the same issue? "They've completely lost touch with not just their voters, but with reality." Here's something else Sey would label fiction — the idea that girls would have to undergo "inappropriate gender verification checks" if there were a national ban on biological males in female sports, as Democrat senator Dick Durbin asserted Wednesday. Sey's counter is that there is already a ban in 27 states, and these verification checks aren't happening. This is unlikely to stop politicians from employing scare tactics, though. And despite the majority of Democrat voters' feelings on the trans-athlete subject, Dansky is skeptical that it will have much of an impact on the midterms. She thinks the Democrats' strategy is to simply ignore this issue and hope Trump's unpopularity will be enough for them to flip the house and senate. Maybe that will work. But this issue isn't going away. Among Wednesday's witnesses was former Australian rules football player Carly Smolak, who testified that a registered sex offender had joined her former team. At a Capitol Hill press conference after the hearing, 17-year-old high school volleyball player Briley Lehcner spoke about a biological male having entered her team's locker room. And last year, Oregon, Washington and California all had state-champion track-and-field athletes that were born male. articles.title: Jeffrey Donaldson victim describes 'profound impact' of child sex abuse
articles.summary: The former DUP leader was found guilty of 18 counts of child sex abuse, including one of rape, in June.
articles.body:
The victims of child sex offender Jeffrey Donaldson have described the impact the abuse had on them.

Donaldson was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one of rape , which he committed against two women when they were children.

The former Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader appeared at Newry Crown Court for a hearing prior to his sentencing in October. He is seeking to appeal his convictions.

The prosecution barrister told the court that one of the women said her childhood had been stolen, while the second said the abuse affected her every day.

In her submission to the pre-sentencing hearing, Rosemary Walsh KC outlined what she described as the "salient facts" that were heard during the course of the trial.

She also described the impact the offending had on both victims, whom were described during the trial as Complainants A and B.

She said both complainants often wondered what life would have been like if they hadn't experienced the abuse.

In her victim impact statement, Complainant A described the "profound impact" the abuse had on her.

Walsh said the complainant believed her childhood had been "stolen" and that she felt an "enormous amount of anger that is always simmering away under the surface".

Walsh said the abuse Complainant B had suffered affected her "every day and every relationship", and that she had to fight on a daily basis the wish that she would die.

Donaldson's defence barrister Keiron Vaughan KC told the court that the 63-year-old was "of previous good character" and that there had been no offending of this type over the last 18 years.

"In that period of time, Mr Donaldson has or did achieve significant things in his life," he said.

"I readily accept that these convictions obliterate all those achievements that he has made in his life, and that's certainly something he will have to live with."

His wife, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, faced a trial of the facts on mental health grounds, meaning she was not required to participate in the proceedings.

She was accused of five related charges, including four counts of aiding and abetting.

She was found to have done the acts of which she was accused – a verdict which she is to appeal.

articles.title: Indian Medical Parliamentarians’ Forum organises National Policy Summit on ‘Swasth bharat se saksham bharat’ to reimagine MedTech access in India
articles.summary: India’s healthcare landscape is evolving rapidly, with medical technology playing an increasingly important role in improving diagnosis, treatment and
articles.body: India’s healthcare landscape is evolving rapidly, with medical technology playing an increasingly important role in improving diagnosis, treatment and patient outcomes. Against this backdrop, and as the country works towards expanding access to quality and affordable healthcare, the Indian Medical Parliamentarians’ Forum (IMPF) convened the National Policy Summit on MedTech Access on September 22 at Meril Academy, Vapi, under the theme ‘Swasth Bharat Se Saksham Bharat | Reimagining MedTech Access in India.’ The summit brought together Members of Parliament, senior government officials, healthcare institutions, clinical experts and industry stakeholders to discuss strengthening India’s medical technology ecosystem and expanding access to quality, advanced and affordable healthcare technologies.Established in 2006, IMPF is a non-partisan platform for Members of Parliament from the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha with backgrounds in medicine and healthcare. The forum promotes evidence-based dialogue on public health priorities and connects parliamentary leadership with government, clinical experts, civil society, academia and industry to support national health policy discussions.The summit was chaired byDr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde, Member of Parliament, Rajya Sabha and Chairperson, IMPF. Senior representatives from the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Department of Health Research, Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, National Health Authority (NHA), AIIMS Nagpur and the National Health Systems Resource Centre (NHSRC) participated.The summit featured two panel discussions bringing together policymakers, healthcare experts, academic leaders and industry representatives to examine the development of India’s MedTech ecosystem and pathways to wider patient access.The first panel, ‘Building a sustainable and globally competitive MedTech ecosystem,’ examined the ecosystem required to support indigenous medical technology development and global competitiveness. Discussions covered research and innovation, regulatory and quality frameworks, industry-academia collaboration, domestic manufacturing, supply-chain resilience and clinical requirements. The panel was chaired by Dr Shivaji Bandappa Kalge, with Shri Manoj Joshi as Co-Chair. Dr Vibhav Garg, Meril, moderated the discussion, with Prof. (Dr.) Prashant P. Joshi and Dr Neha Dumka participating as panellists.The second panel, ‘Expanding access to quality care through MedTech innovation,’ focused on translating medical innovation into meaningful patient access. Discussions covered clinical evidence, health technology assessment, financing and reimbursement, technology adoption, healthcare workforce capabilities and extending advanced technologies across different levels of the health system. The panel was chaired by Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar and moderated by Dr Sharmila Sarkar, with Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan, Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav and Dr Suchita Markan as panellists.Speaking at the summit, Dr Anil Sukhdeorao Bonde said, “Innovation without access has limited impact, and access without evidence cannot be sustained. For India to build a globally competitive medical technology ecosystem, we need stronger indigenous research and development, credible clinical evidence, appropriate health technology assessment and sustainable reimbursement mechanisms. Manufacturing must be supported by the right clinical skills, infrastructure and technical ecosystem. Our ultimate objective must be Indian innovation, global-quality technology and affordable access for every patient who needs it.”Manoj Kumar Joshi, Co-Chair and Secretary, Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, said, “For India to become self-reliant in medical devices, we need a strong ecosystem built around quality, evidence and credibility. Our regulatory system must evolve to ensure products developed in India meet globally credible standards. We also need to strengthen domestic supply chains, engineering capabilities and component manufacturing. This will support healthcare access while contributing to employment and the country’s prosperity.”Highlighting the role of healthcare institutions, Dr Prashant P. Joshi said, “Medical institutions should not be limited to validating technologies developed elsewhere; they should identify unmet clinical needs and work with engineers, researchers and innovators to develop solutions. Stronger collaboration between medical and engineering institutions through joint research, academic programmes, fellowships and training can significantly strengthen India’s medical technology ecosystem.”On clinical adoption and capacity building, Dr Gaurav Shanker Pradhan said, “Access to medical technology is not simply about making a device available. Meaningful impact is possible only when healthcare professionals can use it safely, confidently and effectively. We need to move from an equipment-centric approach to a technology adoption model supported by competency-based training for healthcare professionals.”Dr Shailesh Kumar Yadav, IAS, Joint Director, National Health Authority, highlighted the importance of financing and reimbursement. He said, “For medical technology to reach patients, clinical effectiveness must be supported by appropriate financing and reimbursement pathways. Under Ayushman Bharat, newer interventions require credible clinical and economic evidence before incorporation into health benefit packages. We must also consider the total cost of care rather than only the upfront cost of a device.”Emphasising health-system requirements, Dr Neha Dumka said, “Technology has an important role in strengthening primary healthcare. However, innovation must be assessed for technical capabilities as well as ease of use, cost-effectiveness, scalability and sustainability. Technologies must be capable of effective adoption at different levels of care and ultimately reach the beneficiaries who need them.”Speaking on grassroots healthcare delivery, Dr Jashvantsinh Parmar said, “To take medical technology from innovation to meaningful patient access, we need to identify bottlenecks in the existing system and strengthen the capabilities of healthcare professionals at the grassroots, particularly at CHCs and sub-district centres. Technologies should be introduced systematically and evaluated through comparative, data-based studies.”Highlighting the potential of domestic manufacturers, Dr Shivaji Kalge said, “Indian medical device companies are increasingly capable of developing technologies that meet international standards while remaining affordable for Indian patients. Continued investment in research, quality and innovation can help these technologies gain wider acceptance globally while improving access to quality healthcare.”The summit also included representatives from the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS), National Health Authority, government medical institutions, clinical experts and industry associations.The discussions underscored the need for a coordinated approach spanning indigenous innovation, evidence generation, regulatory quality, clinical education, health technology assessment, financing, reimbursement and institutional adoption, while connecting MedTech innovation with the needs of healthcare providers and patients, particularly in underserved areas.Disclaimer - The above content is non-editorial, and TIL hereby disclaims any and all warranties, expressed or implied, relating to it, and does not guarantee, vouch for or necessarily endorse any of the content.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
