articles.title: Who runs the Election Commission? Three questions at the heart of the dissent row
articles.summary: This week, we are tracking: Two against one, and a server: Who really runs the EC?
articles.body: This week, we are tracking:Two against one, and a server: Who really runs the EC?Trump-Xi meet and Thucydides Trap: The world has turned ChineseNoel vs Chandra: Who will say the final tata?Two golds and a growing tally: India’s Nagoya story so farWho runs the Election Commission? Three questions at the heart of the dissent rowElection Commission is staring at a credibility crisis. The Indian Express report has raised many pertinent questions.Who actually takes decisions inside the EC?As per the IE report, election commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally raised objections at least 14 times over 10 months. These objections were mainly regarding the Special Intensive Revision, voter registration, deletion and restoration of names and control over the electoral-roll database.The EC, in its reply, said: Differences and written observations are normal parts of deliberation and all final decisions over the past year were unanimous.The CEC may be called “Chief”, but legally the Election Commission is a three-member body. Decisions are supposed to be taken unanimously “as far as possible”.Who controls the machinery that controls the voter list?Sandhu and Joshi reportedly questioned whether Electoral Registration Officers had sufficient access and control over ERONet/ECINet. One reported Goa case involved 97 people whom local officials found eligible but who could not immediately be restored because the software lacked the necessary functionality.The EC says centralised digital controls are necessary to prevent unauthorised manipulation and protect database security.Who gets to appoint the umpires?Under the 2023 law, the CEC and Election Commissioners are recommended by a committee consisting of the PM, the leader of opposition and a Union Cabinet minister nominated by the PM.Challenges to the new system are now back before the Supreme Court. On September 23, a two-judge bench split over how the challenge should proceed, with the issue now set to go before a larger bench.What’s nextWhether the issue is appointments, internal decision-making or voter-list software, election administration depends not merely on legal power but on public confidence in how that power is exercised.That is the real debate the EC row has opened up.Read more:When the umpires disagree: 10 questions at the heart of the Election Commission row'Nothing to do with SIR row': EC on postponement of Gyanesh Kumar's outreach programmes in UPEC may order SSR of rolls in Oct for poll-bound statesNoel vs Chandra: Who gets the final say at Tata Sons?Tata Sons on September 24 formally rejected Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata's objection to N Chandrasekaran's reappointment as chairman. The company said the board resolution of September 17 was passed by a majority and followed its Articles of Association.Another vote awaitsThere is a second decision ahead. Shareholders do not have to approve Chandrasekaran’s chairmanship directly, but they must vote on his reappointment as a director at Tata Sons’ annual general meeting. With its controlling stake, Tata Trusts will carry considerable weight there.The listing dilemmaThe leadership fight is tied to a harder question: Must Tata Sons list on the stock market?Tata Trusts opposes a listing, arguing that it would alter a structure in which a charity controls the group and funds its work from dividends. The board agreed to examine ways to comply with RBI rules.The shareholder seeking an exitThe Shapoorji Pallonji group owns about 18.4% of Tata Sons and wants a way to turn part of that holding into cash. It supports a potential listing.Bigger question: This is much bigger than Tata. Our corporate system remains heavily promoter-driven. But modern governance increasingly insists that ownership, board control and management need not be the same thing. So if a promoter owns most of a company, how much right should that confer to control its board?The Tata question now is whether those interests can be reconciled inside the company, or whether a court must settle who has the final say.Read more:Tata Sons tells Noel Tata Chandrasekaran reappointment was legally validN Chandrasekaran's real vote test: Tata Sons AGM, not boardroomEx-CJI, more legal experts back Tata Sons on Chandra's reappointmentTata Sons board unanimous on panel for RBI complianceTrump at the tarmac: When China rules the world“When China rules the world”: Martin Jacques wrote this book in 2012. When this happens, Jacques argued that the world would become more Chinese.It has finally happened. We are living in a Chinese world. Otherwise, who would have thought that an American President would go the airport to receive his Chinese counterpart. But this is what Donald Trump did on September 23 when he went to Joint Base Andrews to personally receive Chines President Xi Jinping.The pageantry was a giveaway of the changing power equations. “For a fleeting moment the changing balance of the US-China relationship was captured not in a joint communique, but in a visual metaphor. As American bombers roared overhead in a flypast intended to wow the visitor, it was Trump who winced, while Xi watched impassively — an unintended piece of geopolitical choreography more eloquent than any statement,” Chidanand Rajghatta wrote in the TOI.All this is happening because Xi is holding a “Trump card” over the US. Xi played this card during the tariff war.Trump is looking for a way out of the Iran war. As per a WSJ report, China is providing military help to Iran. It’s shipping components to be used in drones and missiles.China is increasingly defying US sanctions on Iran. But Trump can’t afford to act against China. Trump is also withholding arms sale to Taiwan to keep Xi in good humour.Thucydides TrapXi called for greater cooperation between US and China to avoid the “Thucydides Trap”. By invoking “Thucydides Trap” again, Xi made it clear that China is equal to US and is on an upward curve. The onus is on the US to accommodate China and not the vice-versa.Read more:Xi Jinping tests Donald Trump with 'Thucydides Trap''Bigger deal' on table: US, China extend trade truce by two months as Xi visits Washington'Let's race, not wrestle': 5 takeaways as Trump-Xi navigate trade, Taiwan and AIWho holds the leverage? Five cards Trump and Xi bring to the tableIndia’s Asian Games medals keep climbing: Where is the gold rush?The medal count is climbing, but India’s Asian Games campaign has a pressing question: How many podium finishes can become gold?By Friday morning at Aichi-Nagoya, India had 19 medals: 2 gold, 8 silver and 9 bronze.Cricket sets the pace: The women’s team retained its title with a 147-run win over Sri Lanka. Then Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh won the 10m air pistol mixed-team event, ending shooting’s wait for gold after a string of close calls.The Hangzhou test: India won a record 106 medals, including 28 gold, in 2023. Nagoya has already produced breakthroughs across sports, alongside a frustrating list of fourth places.We are adding medals every day, but matching Hangzhou will depend on winning more golds before the Games close on October 4.Read more:India one step away from defending kabaddi gold medals as men and women storm into finalsIndia's medal tally hits 20; Manush Shah, Diya Chitale win mixed doubles table tennis bronze'15 years ... articles.title: Five unauthorised health centres near MMCH sealed
articles.summary: Five unauthorised health centres near MMCH Daltonganj were sealed after an inspection found violations of the Clinical Establishment Act and poor sample handling.
articles.body: Daltonganj: Five unauthorised health facilities operating near MMCH Daltonganj were ordered to be sealed on Friday following a surprise inspection led by Palamu DC Dilip Pratap Singh Shekhawat, sources said.The facilities, including four pathological sample-collection centres and a clinic, were found operating in violation of the Clinical Establishment Act.Civil surgeon Dr Anil Kumar Srivastava, who accompanied the DC during the inspection, said the collection centres lacked adequate space, trained staff and valid registration. “There was hardly any space for patients to wait, and the centres had no legal documents showing a tie-up with a licensed diagnostic laboratory,” he said.The centres were also found to have inadequate arrangements for the collection, storage and handling of blood, urine and other pathological samples. Bio-medical waste management was another major concern, sources said.The clinic was sealed for failing to produce documentary proof of registration under the Act, the civil surgeon said.Asked whether the presence of unauthorised centres near MMCH reflected poorly on senior health officials, Shekhawat said such lapses were a matter of concern and warned that no one would be allowed to violate health regulations with impunity.Stay updated with the latest Ranchi news. articles.title: Met should probe handling of 'Putney Pusher' suspect death, says IOPC
articles.summary: Nicholas Brandram's family say he took his own life due to the "pressure" of a police investigation.
articles.body:
The police watchdog has said the Metropolitan Police's professional standards unit should investigate the force's handling of a case in which a man suspected of pushing a woman into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge was found dead.

Nicholas Brandram was found dead at his London home on 15 September. His family said he took his own life after the "immense pressure" of a police investigation .

The 44-year-old was under suspicion of being the jogger who pushed a woman into the path of a bus during a run on Putney Bridge in west London in May 2017.

The Met police made a mandatory referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) following the banker's death.

In a statement, the IOPC said: "After carefully considering the referral, we have decided that an investigation is required and that the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards should conduct it.

"We have recommended the review considers matters including the necessity and proportionality of arrest, what engagement was there with the media and considerations made in relation to Mr Brandram's welfare and the relevant policy."

The police watchdog added that if the Met's investigation did not find "any potential misconduct", the final report must be submitted to the IOPC for review.

The family of Nicholas Brandram insisted in an interview with the BBC that he was not the so-called "Putney pusher".

Ch Sup Dan Knowles said he recognised the "strain that being subject to a police investigation" could cause.

He confirmed that the Met's Directorate of Professional Standards would carry out the investigation.

The force said the investigation into the 2017 incident remained ongoing.

articles.title: Man shot during 2024 Trump campaign rally in Butler dies
articles.summary: A gunman shot Jim Copenhaver twice while also killing another man and grazing Trump's ear with a bullet.
articles.body:
One of the three attendees who was shot at Donald Trump's 2024 presidential campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, has passed away from complications stemming from his injuries, according to the Pennsylvania attorney general.

Jim Copenhaver, 76, was struck twice when a gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop. Another attendee, Corey Comperatore, was killed in the shooting and Trump's ear was grazed by a bullet.

Copenhaver died on Wednesday at a hospital in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner shared with local media.

The gunman, 20-year-old Thomas Crooks, was killed by Secret Service after he opened fire.

In a post on his social media site Truth Social, Trump called Copenhaver a "true American patriot".

"More than two years ago in Butler, Pennsylvania, a crazed gunman attempted to stifle our America First Movement. Instead, Jim and so many other wonderful Patriots who love our Country, stood united in defense of our shared values of Freedom, Liberty, and Justice," Trump said. "Our hearts and prayers are with the Copenhaver family, especially his incredible wife Marianne."

An attorney for Copenhaver's family said his dedication to the US was a "defining part of his life".

"As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered," the lawyer said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News.

In an interview with CBS a year after the Butler rally, Copenhaver and David Dutch, the third attendee who was shot, said they had been through infections and surgeries after being wounded.

Copenhaver was shot in the arm and the abdomen. A year later, the bullet was still lodged in his body next to his spine, he told CBS, causing him to walk with a cane.

Both Dutch and Copenhaver sued the federal government for damages in June, arguing the Secret Service failed to ensure their safety and was therefore liable for their injuries.

Republicans in the US House of Representatives also paid tribute to Copenhaver on Friday, saying in a social media post: "Jim endured unimaginable hardship with strength and perseverance."

articles.title: A Nebraska couple lost a mortgage-free home assessed at $59,759 after a $588.21 tax debt grew to $5,268.32; the US Supreme Court sent the case back and Nebraska's top court revived the compensation claim
articles.summary: A legal fight over homeownership and tax liens in Nebraska reached a major turning point when the state's highest court revived a compensation claim from
articles.body: A legal fight over homeownership and tax liens in Nebraska reached a major turning point when the state's highest court revived a compensation claim from a couple who lost their mortgage-free home over a relatively small tax debt. Kevin Fair and his wife, Terry, owned a home in Scotts Bluff County with no mortgage or other liens. The property was valued by the county at $59,759. After the couple failed to pay $588.21 in property taxes, the county sold the tax debt to Continental Resources. The dispute eventually reached the US Supreme Court before returning to the Nebraska Supreme Court. In 2024, the Nebraska court ruled that Fair had a valid claim that he was deprived of property without just compensation.Debt swells and deed changes handsThe case began in 2015, when the Scotts Bluff County treasurer sold a tax certificate for the unpaid $588.21 to Continental Resources on March 11. Nebraska law allowed the county to sell the tax certificate to a private buyer. Continental then paid later property taxes on the home. The county stopped sending the Fairs further tax bills after Continental began making those payments. Three years later, on April 13, 2018, Continental sent the couple a “Notice of Expiration of Right of Redemption.” The notice gave them three months to recover the property by paying $5,268, which represented the unpaid taxes, interest, fees, and other costs. The Fairs did not pay the amount within the three-month period. In July 2018, Continental applied for a tax deed, and the county treasurer issued the deed to the company. At that time, the county assessed the property at $59,759. The deed transferred the property to Continental free of the Fairs' ownership interest.District court and initial appealsContinental then filed a quiet title case in state court to establish its ownership. Kevin Fair responded with a counterclaim and a third-party complaint against Scotts Bluff County and the county treasurer. The Nebraska Attorney General also took part because Fair was challenging the constitutionality of state laws. Fair argued that taking a property worth $59,759 to satisfy a tax debt of $5,268 amounted to an unconstitutional taking without just compensation under both the US and Nebraska Constitutions. He also raised claims under the Due Process Clauses, the Excessive Fines Clause of the US Constitution, and other provisions of the Nebraska Constitution. The District Court for Scotts Bluff County granted summary judgment for Continental and rejected Fair's constitutional claims. Fair appealed. In 2022, the Nebraska Supreme Court initially upheld the lower court's decision, ruling that Nebraska's tax certificate system was not unconstitutional in the ways Fair had argued.US Supreme Court intervenesFair then asked the US Supreme Court to review the case. While that request was pending, the US Supreme Court decided Tyler v. Hennepin County in 2023. In Tyler, the Court held that a homeowner could have a constitutional takings claim when a government takes property to pay a tax debt and keeps the property's value above the amount owed. The US Supreme Court later granted review in Fair's case, vacated the Nebraska Supreme Court's earlier ruling, and sent the case back to Nebraska for reconsideration in light of Tyler v. Hennepin County. The case remained docketed as S-21-074.State supreme court revives claimAfter reviewing the case again, the Nebraska Supreme Court reversed the lower court's summary judgment on Fair's takings claim. The decision was issued on August 23, 2024, in Continental Resources v. Fair, 317 Neb. 391. According to the Nebraska Supreme Court's opinion, Fair had a protected property interest in the value of his home above the amount of his tax debt. The court said that if the property was worth more than the debt, taking that extra value without paying Fair could amount to a taking without just compensation. The court also concluded that Continental could potentially be responsible for paying that compensation. The justices found that Continental's decision to seek the tax deed was sufficiently connected to the state tax system to count as state action for purposes of Fair's takings claim. The court therefore sent that claim back for further proceedings. The court did not revive Fair's other constitutional claims. It upheld summary judgment for Continental and the county on those claims, including the Excessive Fines claim.Impact on local tax practicesUnder the Nebraska tax certificate system that applied in 2015, a county could sell a tax certificate for unpaid property taxes to a private buyer. If the owner did not redeem the property within the required period, the certificate holder could seek a tax deed and obtain the property. The Nebraska Supreme Court noted that the laws governing this process were substantially changed in later years. The court's 2024 ruling did not award Fair a specific amount of money. Instead, it found that genuine factual issues remained over his claim for just compensation and sent the case back to the district court for further proceedings. The court also ruled that Scotts Bluff County was entitled to summary judgment on that claim, while leaving the question of possible state liability undecided.You use AI every day.
